_comment: Per-country connectivity facts for /tools/esim pages. English source of truth; prose fields (intro, coverage, tips) are translated by scripts/translate-esim.mjs into src/i18n/esim-i18n.json with a srcHash stamp, so editing a field here re-queues its translations. EVERGREEN FACTS ONLY: carrier names and coverage character — never prices, plan sizes or vendor claims (those go stale and we link to live pricing instead). Keyed by countries.json slug; a country gets an eSIM page when it is active in countries.json AND has an entry here.

japan.name: Japan
japan.intro: Japan runs on four nationwide networks — NTT Docomo, au (KDDI), SoftBank and the newer Rakuten Mobile. Travel eSIMs almost always ride one of the big three, and for a visitor the practical difference between them is small: all three are fast and dependable in the places tourists actually go.
japan.coverage: City coverage is superb, and unusually for the world, that includes the underground — you keep a signal on Tokyo and Osaka metro platforms and inside most trains. Coverage follows the shinkansen lines well. Where it thins out is deep in the mountains: remote onsen valleys, high hiking trails and some stretches of rural Hokkaido can drop to weak or no signal, so download offline maps before a countryside day trip.
tips: Japan is still surprisingly cash-based, but it is also map-app-dependent: addresses are hard to navigate without data, so a working connection matters more here than in most countries.
Free WiFi exists in convenience stores, hotels and many stations, but it is patchy and login-walled on the street — plan on mobile data rather than hopping between hotspots.
Train-planning apps (route search, platform numbers, delays) are the single biggest data use for visitors — make sure your plan has enough data for heavy map and transit use.
Airport SIM counters and vending machines exist at the major airports, but after a long-haul landing the queue and the paperwork are exactly what an eSIM installed at home lets you skip.

thailand.name: Thailand
thailand.intro: Thailand's mobile market is dominated by two big networks: AIS, the largest, and True, which absorbed dtac in their 2023 merger. Most travel eSIMs connect through one of these two, and both are strong in every place on a normal tourist route.
thailand.coverage: Bangkok, Chiang Mai and the coastal cities have fast, dense coverage, and the popular islands — Phuket, Samui, Phangan, Krabi's beaches — are well served in towns and resort areas. Signal gets patchy on remote beaches, in national parks and in the mountainous border regions, so treat a jungle trek or a far-flung island cove as offline time.
tips: Daily life for a visitor runs on data: Grab for rides, translation apps at street stalls, and QR codes everywhere — Thailand is one of the most QR-payment-heavy countries you will visit.

Tourist SIM counters at Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports are famous and genuinely fine — but they meet every long-haul arrival wave, so an eSIM installed before departure saves you the one queue you least want after a red-eye.
Island-hopping? Coverage is best in populated areas; boats between islands and quiet stretches of coast can be dead zones, so download tickets and maps before you leave WiFi.
If your trip includes long bus or train legs (Bangkok–Chiang Mai, the southern lines), coverage along the routes is decent but variable — download entertainment in advance.

vietnam.name: Vietnam
vietnam.intro: Vietnam has three main networks — Viettel, Vinaphone and MobiFone. Viettel, run with military-grade ambition, is the largest and has the strongest rural footprint; the other two are solid in cities and towns. Which network a travel eSIM uses matters more here than in most countries, precisely because of that rural gap.
vietnam.coverage: Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang and every provincial city are well covered with fast data. The differences show up in the mountains and the countryside: the Ha Giang loop, Sapa's valleys and remote stretches of the central highlands are where Viettel keeps a bar or two while others fade. On the classic north–south route the populated corridor is fine on any network.
tips: Grab (rides) and a translation app are near-essential in Vietnam, and both are useless without data — get connected before you need your first ride from the airport.
Doing the Ha Giang loop, Sapa treks or other mountain riding? Prefer a plan on Viettel's network and still expect dead zones on the passes — download offline maps.
Buying a physical SIM locally means passport registration at the counter; an eSIM bought before the trip skips the paperwork entirely.
Hotel and café WiFi is everywhere and genuinely fast in cities — your data plan mostly needs to cover the hours in between, so mid-sized plans go further than you might expect.
